output.title: Skin-irritation / adhesion tag cluster — review against known open adhesive-lift mechanism
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the ticket rise to the known general adhesive-lift mechanism (high motion intensity plus elevated skin-temp delta) rather than a new lot/firmware defect. Motion_intensity rose only marginally and skin_temp_delta_c fell between windows, so the mechanism's own drivers are not clearly elevated despite the ticket increase, leaving the explanation unconfirmed. A falsifying test is to check whether adhesion_flag increases are concentrated in the high-activity_level cohort; if not, the mechanism cannot explain the observed rise, and a lot- or firmware-specific defect becomes the more consistent explanation. Status is downgraded to INCONCLUSIVE pending that breakdown.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The current skin-irritation/adhesion ticket cluster is most consistent with continuation of the already-open, general adhesive-lift mechanism (elevated during high motion intensity and patch-site temperature delta), rather than a new firmware- or lot-specific defect, based on flat-to-mild telemetry movement and no firmware-linked rate difference.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The rise in skin-irritation/adhesion tickets reflects a new, lot- or batch-specific adhesive defect (as in INC-2025-031) rather than the general motion/temperature-driven adhesion-lift mechanism, and would not require elevated motion_intensity or skin_temp_delta_c to explain the ticket increase.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull the adhesion_flag rate broken down by activity_level for the current window: if the rate increase is not concentrated in the high-activity_level segment (i.e., flag rates rise similarly or more in low/medium-activity cohorts), the motion-intensity-driven mechanism cannot account for the observed rise, falsifying the leading hypothesis.

deterministic_findings.label: adhesion_flag rate ratio, firmware one point four point zero vs one point four point two, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Sampled current-window and prior-window skin-irritation tickets co-occur with adhesion and comfort-fit tags and describe patch lift during high-intensity sessions, matching the documented adhesion-lift symptom profile.

The known issues register documents an open, general mechanism where lift rates rise with high motion intensity and elevated skin_temp_delta_c, and instructs against closing new clusters as expected without a lot check.
The support playbook instructs that adhesion-tagged clusters must be escalated to operations rather than closed as a known-issue wave-away.

counter_evidence.claim: skin_temp_delta_c, the telemetry proxy for the documented risk driver, decreased slightly from the prior to the current window rather than increasing.

Comparing adhesion_flag rates between the two firmware versions in the current window shows a ratio near one with a confidence interval that spans one, indicating no detectable firmware-specific effect.

motion_intensity, the second telemetry proxy the known-issue register ties to the adhesive-lift mechanism, rose only marginally between windows, while skin_temp_delta_c actually fell, so neither of the two documented drivers shows the clear joint elevation the mechanism requires even as ticket volume rose.

The current-window skin-irritation feedback sample spans multiple firmware versions (1.4.2, 1.2.0, 1.4.0, 1.3.0) and regions (nordics, dach, benelux), which is consistent with either a broad general mechanism or a lot defect distributed across a mixed device population; sample size is too small to distinguish the two.

output.title: Overheating tag cluster in Nordics traced to known benign cold-weather battery/UI pattern
output.summary: Direct query confirms all overheating-tagged feedback records in the current window ({f_4}) are Nordics-only and co-tagged with battery/app-ui, and region-level skin_temp_delta_c shows Nordics tracking closely with every other region (no elevation), which is consistent with rather than falsifying the leading hypothesis. The falsifying test is: an overheating record outside Nordics, or without battery/app-ui co-tags, or elevated skin_temp_delta_c for the specific devices involved, would break the claim that this is entirely the benign cold-weather mislabel pattern.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The overheating tag cluster reflects the previously characterized Nordics cold-weather battery drain pattern (KI-NW-014) plus an alarming app sync/battery UI screen, misdescribed by users as overheating, rather than a real thermal or hardware issue; skin temperature telemetry does not track with these reports.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The overheating tag reflects a genuine thermal effect confined to a specific firmware or device subset within Nordics that is masked when skin_temp_delta_c is aggregated at the regional level, so region-wide flat rates do not rule out a localized hardware issue.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: If any overheating-tagged feedback record occurs outside the Nordics region, or without co-occurring battery/app-ui tags, or if skin_temp_delta_c for the specific devices/firmware named in overheating tickets is elevated relative to the regional baseline in {f_1}, the leading hypothesis (that this is entirely the Nordics cold-weather battery/UI mislabel pattern) cannot hold.

deterministic_findings.label: skin_temp_delta_c rate ratio, firmware 1.4.1 vs 1.4.2, Nordics, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: All sampled overheating feedback records in both windows are from the Nordics region and co-tagged with battery and app-ui, with text describing cold-weather battery drain and warm-feeling phones during sync or alarming UI screens, not device thermal events.

The knowledge base documents KI-NW-014 as a standing, accepted Nordics battery-drain characteristic present since early firmware and not introduced by the latest firmware, with skin_temp_delta_c correlation to battery_drain_pct near zero in Nordics device-days.
Support playbook guidance instructs treating Nordics cold-weather battery/warmth tickets as known regional behaviour rather than opening hardware incidents by default.

counter_evidence.claim: A prior incident closing Nordics winter drain tickets as not-an-incident still notes that a future global drain step or single-device step would be a different shape and should not be dismissed reflexively.

All current-window overheating-tagged records ({f_4}) are from Nordics and are co-tagged with battery and app-ui, and skin_temp_delta_c broken down by region shows no elevation in Nordics relative to any other region, consistent with the leading hypothesis rather than refuting it.
